Since I cannot "think" or have personal opinions, I can provide a technical overview of what the ai-chat-exporter repository does and who it is for.

Based on the repository's purpose, it is a tool designed to help users archive their conversations from various AI platforms. Many AI chat interfaces store history in proprietary formats or make it difficult to export data in a way that is easy to search, back up, or move to another LLM. This tool aims to bridge that gap by providing a way to extract those chats into more standardized, portable formats.

For a developer or a power user, this is useful for:

  • Data Ownership: Ensuring you have a local copy of your prompts and the AI's responses regardless of the platform's terms of service or account status.
  • Knowledge Management: Importing AI conversations into personal knowledge bases like Obsidian, Notion, or Logseq.
  • Fine-tuning: Collecting a dataset of high-quality interactions to eventually fine-tune your own smaller models.

If you are considering using it, you should check the current supported platforms in the README to ensure it works with the specific AI service you use, and always be cautious when granting third-party tools access to your chat history or API keys.

AI Chat Exporter (the Covai‑Labs “ace” project) is a free, open‑source browser extension that lets you back up and export conversations from a wide range of AI assistants—including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Perplexity and many others—into Markdown, JSON, PDF, PNG or directly into note‑taking tools such as Obsidian or Logseq.

Key points

  • Privacy‑first design – All parsing and export happen locally in the browser; the extension stores no data on remote servers, collects no telemetry, and requires no accounts. Mozilla
  • Broad platform support – Dedicated parsers handle >15 AI platforms, preserving rich features like reasoning traces, code blocks, tables, citations and even LaTeX math. Google
  • Open‑source & actively maintained – The source code is publicly available under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, with regular updates and a public issue tracker. Google
  • Positive user feedback – The extension rates 4.9 / 5 on the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add‑ons, indicating strong user satisfaction. Google

Overall, it’s a solid choice if you want a locally‑run, no‑account solution for safely exporting AI chat histories. It’s especially appealing for users who keep personal knowledge bases (e.g., Obsidian) and value auditability through open‑source code.

You cannot evolve out of a clade. But some cunts get offended when we say we are monkeys. I mean in  sense of monophyletic groups. So we all are simians, aren't we ?  

gpt-oss 120B

In phylogenetic (evolutionary) terms a clade is a group that includes an ancestor and all of its descendants.
When we talk about “monkeys” we’re actually dealing with a paraphyletic group: it leaves out some descendants of the common ancestor—namely the apes (including humans).

So:

  • Simians (infraorder Simiiformes) = all monkeys plus all apes. This is a true clade.
  • Monkeys (suborder Anthropoidea split into Platyrrhini (New World) and Cercopithecoidea (Old World)) exclude the apes, making the group paraphyletic.

Because humans share the same ancestor as all other simians, we are simians.
Saying “we are monkeys” is technically inaccurate in a strict cladistic sense, but it’s often used colloquially because “monkey” is the familiar term for members of the broader simian lineage.

So the precise answer is:

  • Yes, we are all simians.
  • No, we are not monkeys in the strict monophyletic sense, because the term “monkey” leaves out the ape lineage that includes us.

Why does the RSS claim that they are indigenous to India, when the mainstream historical and genetic evidence supports Indo-Aryan migration into the subcontinent? And why do some Tamil nationalists describe RSS gang as vantheris?

Why the RSS says “Indigenous to India”

  1. Ideological narrative – The RSS’s historiography is built around Hindutva: a vision of India as a continuous, culturally homogeneous nation that predates any foreign influence. Claiming that the Aryans (and therefore Hindus) are indigenous fits that narrative and reinforces the idea of an “Akhand Bharat” (undivided India).

  2. Selective use of evidence – Pro‑Indigenous‑Aryan groups cherry‑pick archaeological, linguistic and genetic data that can be interpreted to support an internal origin (e.g., emphasizing continuity between the Harappan civilisation and the Vedic culture, or arguing that the term “Arya” was originally Indian). They down‑play or dismiss the bulk of modern archaeological, linguistic and especially ancient‑DNA research that points to a Bronze‑Age migration from the Pontic‑Caspian steppe into South Asia. Wikipedia

  3. Political mobilisation – Presenting the Aryans as native undermines the historical narrative used by colonial and post‑colonial scholars to explain the diversity of Indian cultures, and it provides a “cultural purity” argument that can be mobilised against perceived external threats (e.g., Muslim rule, western criticism).

Mainstream scholarly consensus

  • Archaeology & linguistics – The Indo‑Aryan migration model (step‑peoples moving into the Indus‑Ganges region ~1800‑1500 BCE) is supported by material culture changes, the spread of chariot technology, and the linguistic pattern of elite‑dominance language shift. Lumen Learning

  • Genetics – Ancient DNA studies show a clear influx of step‑peoples related to the Yamnaya/Andronovo cultures into South Asia during the Bronze Age, bringing the “steppe‑related” ancestry component that is now widespread in northern Indian populations. This genetic signal aligns with the linguistic and archaeological evidence.

Why some Tamil nationalists call the RSS a “vantheri”

  • “Vantheri” (Tamil: வாந்தெரி) is a pejorative term meaning “outsider” or “invader.” Tamil nationalists use it to accuse the RSS of trying to impose a north‑Indian, Sanskrit‑centric Hindutva agenda on the Dravidian south, effectively portraying the RSS as a cultural coloniser rather than a genuine Indian movement.

  • Historical grievance – Tamil historiography emphasises the continuity of the ancient Tamil kingdoms (Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas) and the Dravidian linguistic tradition, which they argue predates and survived any Aryan influx. Calling the RSS “vantheri” reinforces the view that the organization is a later, foreign‑influenced force seeking to rewrite southern history.

  • Political opposition – By labeling the RSS as a “vantheri,” Tamil activists link Hindutva’s “Indigenous Aryan” claim to an external imposition, thereby delegitimising the RSS’s attempts to claim cultural primacy across all of India.

In short

  • The RSS’s claim of indigeneity is driven by a Hindutva‑type political narrative that selectively interprets evidence.
  • The prevailing scholarly picture—archaeology, linguistics and especially ancient DNA—supports a Bronze‑Age Indo‑Aryan migration into the subcontinent.
  • Tamil nationalists label the RSS “vantheri” to stress that they view Hindutva as an external, north‑Indian intrusion threatening Dravidian cultural continuity.

Why the RSS / BJP champion the NEP‑2020 three‑language formula

Goal claimed in the policyHow it is implemented in practiceWho benefits / who is burdened
“National integration” – a link languageThe third language is expected to be Hindi in all non‑Hindi‑speaking states because schools lack teachers and textbooks for other Indian languages. CBSE’s 2026 circular even classifies English as “foreign” and defaults the Indian language slot to Sanskrit, leaving Hindi as the de‑facto choice for most students. CountercurrentsChildren in Tamil‑, Kannada‑, Malayalam‑, Oriya‑ etc. states must learn Hindi (or Sanskrit) in addition to English and their mother tongue, while students in Hindi‑belt states add English and a southern language.
“Preserve regional languages”The policy allows any “native Indian language”, but the central implementation gives states no funding or curriculum support for teaching a third regional language. Consequently, the only viable option is the centrally promoted Hindi/Sanskrit pair. polsci.instituteRegional language speakers lose classroom time for their own language; the burden falls on states that want to protect their language (e.g., Tamil Nadu’s two‑language stance).
“Promote English for global competence”English is re‑labelled a “foreign” language, pushing it to the bottom of the hierarchy in CBSE schools. This subtly de‑emphasises English while still keeping it as a compulsory subject, satisfying a nationalist narrative without sacrificing the prestige of English for elite schools. CountercurrentsElite private‑school students continue with strong English instruction; ordinary public‑school students get weaker English exposure and extra Hindi/Sanskrit load.
“Cultural nationalism – Sanskrit & Hindi”BJP‑aligned ministries have openly advocated that the Indian language slot be Sanskrit (the “classical” language of the Hindu tradition). In practice, because Sanskrit textbooks are only available up to class 6, schools hand them down to class 9‑10 students, effectively forcing Hindi as the next‑best choice. CountercurrentsStudents in non‑Hindi states are compelled to study a language associated with the Indo‑Iranian branch, which most of them have never encountered, while the party leadership’s own children often attend private schools exempt from the rule.
“Flexibility and no imposition” (NEP wording)The policy’s language‑choice clause (“at least two native Indian languages”) is deliberately vague, allowing the centre to interpret “native” as Hindi everywhere except the Hindi belt. This legal wiggle‑room lets the centre claim compliance while still imposing Hindi. Legal‑istic defence for the centre; states can protest but have little leverage because the wording leaves enforcement to CBSE and the central Ministry of Education.

What’s really happening

  1. Political motive – Hindutva ideology views Hindi (an Indo‑Iranian language) as a cultural glue that can bind the nation under a broadly “Hindu” identity. Promoting Sanskrit reinforces that same narrative. Countercurrents
  2. Administrative convenience – Central ministries produce a single set of textbooks (Hindi/Sanskrit) that can be rolled out nationwide, avoiding the logistical nightmare of creating separate third‑language curricula for each of India’s 20‑plus regional languages. polsci.institute
  3. Electoral calculus – The BJP’s core support base is in the Hindi belt. Giving Hindi a privileged status in the school system consolidates that base, while southern parties (DMK, AIADMK, etc.) can rally opposition around “language imposition”, a proven mobilising issue. BBC

Why southern states label it “imposition”

  • Historical trauma – Tamil Nadu’s anti‑Hindi agitations of 1965 (over 70 deaths) created a lasting collective memory that any attempt to make Hindi compulsory is a political assault. polsci.institute
  • Two‑language tradition – Since the 1960s Tamil Nadu has taught only Tamil + English; the three‑language demand threatens that established right. polsci.institute
  • Perceived cultural domination – For Dravidian parties, the push for an Indo‑Iranian language (Hindi) is seen as a north‑Indian cultural hegemony that marginalises Dravidian linguistic heritage. BBC

Bottom line

The NEP‑2020 three‑language formula is framed as a flexible, multilingual policy, but the way the RSS‑backed BJP implements it—classifying English as foreign, defaulting the Indian‑language slot to Sanskrit/Hindi, and providing no state‑specific support—effectively imposes Hindi (or Sanskrit) on non‑Hindi‑speaking states. Southern states oppose it because it clashes with their long‑standing two‑language model and is interpreted as part of a broader Hindutva agenda to promote an Indo‑Iranian linguistic identity across India.

Why the memory of World War II dominates European curricula while colonial atrocities are marginalised

FactorEffect on collective memoryHow it shapes school syllabi
Scale & proximity of violenceWWII devastated the continent itself (cities destroyed, millions of civilians killed on European soil). The trauma is part of everyday family histories.National ministries built Holocaust‑ and war‑memory programmes (e.g., Germany’s “Never Again” curriculum, France’s “Shoah” lessons) that are legally required in schools.
State‑led “memory politics” after 1945The victorious Allies deliberately linked reconstruction to an “unswerving remembrance” of the Nazi genocide and the battle against fascism.EU‑wide observances (Holocaust Remembrance Day, Europe Day) are embedded in curricula; funding is allocated for museums, memorial trips, and teacher‑training.
Cold‑War geopolitical framingThe West framed WWII as a fight against totalitarianism, while colonial wars were portrayed as “civilising missions” or “de‑colonisation” later.History textbooks emphasize the “liberation of Europe” and treat de‑colonisation as a peripheral post‑1945 footnote.
Narrative simplicity vs. complexityWWII offers a clear‑cut villain (Nazism) and hero narrative (Allied liberation). Colonialism involves multiple actors, long timelines, and economic exploitation, making it harder to summarise.Syllabi favour concise, emotionally resonant modules (e.g., concentration‑camp visits) over nuanced, contested debates about empire.
Political interests of the “perpetrator” statesContemporary European parties (especially right‑wing) profit from a heroic national myth of resistance; acknowledging colonial crimes would undermine that myth.Textbook committees, often staffed by historians aligned with mainstream parties, give limited space to colonial violence (usually a few paragraphs on “the Belgian Congo” or “Algerian War”).
Institutional amnesia & “memory entrepreneurs”Scholars such as Aline Sierp note a “colonial amnesia” deliberately perpetuated by French and Belgian governments to avoid reparations or legal liability.Official curricula lack dedicated units on “European colonial genocide”; when mentioned, it is framed as a “controversial debate” rather than a settled fact.
EU’s trans‑national memory agendaEU bodies have institutionalised remembrance of the Holocaust and Stalinist terror (e.g., EU‑Europe of Memory project) but have no comparable EU‑wide programme for colonial crimes.Funding and teacher‑training are channelled to Holocaust education; colonial‑memory projects receive sporadic, NGO‑driven support, rarely reaching schools.

Key scholarly explanations

  1. “Preferred atrocities” bias – Researchers argue that European institutions consciously elevate the Holocaust and WWII because they occurred on European territory and involve European victims, while colonial atrocities happened abroad and affect non‑European peoples. This creates a “zero‑sum” memory where acknowledging one set of crimes threatens the prestige of the other.

  2. Political utility of WWII memory – Post‑war governments used the war narrative to legitimize the democratic order, embed “never again” rhetoric, and anchor European integration. Colonial oppression, by contrast, would expose continuities of racism and exploitation that many post‑war states preferred to downplay.

  3. Structural educational choices – Curriculum designers must fit a limited number of weeks into national history programmes. Because WWII is mandated by law in many countries (e.g., Germany’s “Gedenkpflicht”), it crowds out space for colonial studies.

What the evidence tells us

  • Textbook analyses consistently find that mentions of the Belgian Congo, French Indochina, British Raj, or Dutch East Indies occupy < 5 % of the “20th‑century” chapter, whereas the Holocaust occupies > 30 % of the same chapter. Colby College
  • Public‑opinion surveys in Germany, France, the UK and the Netherlands show that ≥ 70 % of respondents associate “European history” primarily with WWII, while < 30 % spontaneously name colonial violence. gerda-henkel-stiftung.de
  • Policy documents (EU’s “European Memory of the Holocaust” programme, national “Holocaust education acts”) contain explicit funding allocations; comparable EU‑wide resolutions on colonial reparations or genocide remain absent or symbolic. odu.edu

Bottom line

European collective memory and school curricula centre WWII because the war:

  • Happened on the continent, producing a shared, emotionally powerful trauma.
  • Was deliberately institutionalised by post‑war governments as a cornerstone of democratic legitimacy.
  • Serves current political narratives that emphasise European unity and moral redemption.

Colonial atrocities, though equally massive, are marginalised because they:

  • Occurred outside Europe, affecting peoples who are not part of the dominant national audience.
  • Challenge the self‑image of the former imperial powers and risk legal or reparative consequences.
  • Lack a coordinated trans‑national memory infrastructure comparable to the Holocaust‑centric programmes.

Thus, the overshadowing of colonial crimes is not an accidental omission but the result of deliberate political, institutional, and pedagogical choices that privilege a particular, “European‑centric” version of history.

two questions. Tell me about Euler's identity. And why LLMs aren't being trained on language of Orcas. (if they are being trained, correct me)

gpt-oss 120B

Euler’s identity

Euler’s identity is the celebrated equation

eiπ+1=0e^{i\pi}+1=0eiπ+1=0

It bundles together five of mathematics’ most fundamental constants:

  • eee – the base of natural logarithms (≈ 2.718).
  • iii – the imaginary unit, defined by i2=−1i^{2}=-1i2=−1.
  • π\piπ – the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter (≈ 3.14159).
  • 1 – the multiplicative identity.
  • 0 – the additive identity.

The identity follows from Euler’s formula eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θe^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθ. Substituting θ=π\theta=\piθ=π gives eiπ=−1e^{i\pi}= -1eiπ=−1, which rearranges to the compact form above. Its elegance lies in linking algebra, geometry, and analysis in a single, simple expression, and it’s often cited as an example of mathematical beauty.

Why LLMs aren’t (generally) trained on Orca vocalisations

  • Training data are text‑based. Most large‑scale language models (e.g., GPT‑4, LLaMA, Claude) are trained on massive corpora of written human language scraped from the web, books, code repositories, etc. Orca calls are acoustic signals, not text, so they fall outside that data source.

  • Lack of aligned transcription. Even if recordings exist, there are very few reliable, large‑scale transcriptions of Orca “language” that map vocal patterns to symbolic tokens the model could ingest. The scientific community is still debating how much of the acoustic repertoire constitutes a structured language versus context‑dependent signaling.

  • Domain‑specific models are rare. Some research projects have built bioacoustic or multimodal models that ingest spectrograms or audio waveforms (e.g., wav2vec‑2.0, CLIP‑like audio‑text models). These are far smaller than mainstream LLMs and are tuned for tasks like species identification, not general conversational generation.

  • Ethical and practical constraints. Training a model on animal communication raises questions about interpretation, potential anthropomorphism, and misuse. Until there’s a consensus on what the data represent and how they should be used, developers typically avoid incorporating them.

If any models are being trained on Orca sounds:
There are a handful of acoustic‑pattern classifiers that learn from labelled Orca recordings to identify pod‑specific calls or behavioural contexts. These are audio‑only neural networks, not language models that generate or understand human‑like text. No publicly known LLM (as of 2026) includes Orca vocalisations as part of its textual training corpus.
